A rise in a fixed-rate bond's yield lowe.why: A textbook rule stated in this general form hundreds of times; it follows arithmetically from pricing a bond as the present value of fixed cash flows, with no exceptions for fixed cash flows and a positive yield.

bond prices and yields move in opposite directions

price of a bond falls when its yield rises

The US 10-year Treasury note is a fixed-.why: Treasury price and yield are reported together daily, so the member's own fact ('Treasury prices fell as yields rose') is stored directly: the by-name route.

sources.quote: Ordinary Treasury notes pay a fixed interest rate that is set at auction.

Germany's 10-year Bund is a fixed-rate b.why: Bund yields are reported very often ('Bund yields' 9,010) but the member's price fact much less often ('Bund prices fell' 11), so the by-name route is weaker here than for Treasuries: a lopsided pair.

notes: The rule has no exception for fixed cash flows and a positive yield (price is the present value of the cash flows, decreasing in the discount rate). Worlds combine two independent storage choices (Treasury note, Bund). In a by-name world the member's stored price fact wins and its membership gives way (it no longer counts as a fixed-rate bond); it never stays a fixed-rate bond as an exception to the rule, which would be the inconsistent patch (README Decisions 2). Derivability very_unlikely: the rule is stated directly and follows from no subclass chain. Plausibility: price and yield moving together is a common confusion, and clearly false.
